a: His name was Lazarus
p: Lazarus is the Greek form of Eleazar, "God has helped." Only John tells his story.
b: Lazaros is a short Greek form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, "God has helped," one of the most common Jewish names of the time. He is not the beggar Lazarus of Jesus' parable (Luke 16:19–31), though some scholars think the two stories are connected (see the chapter page). Luke knows Martha and Mary, the active sister and the listening sister, but does not name their village or mention a brother (Luke 10:38–42). Only John tells of Lazarus. This Bethany, just outside Jerusalem (11:18), is a different place from "Bethany on the far side of the Jordan," where John baptized and where Jesus is staying when the message comes (1:28; 10:40).

a: This was the Mary who anointed the Lord
t: Which Mary? Three women who became one
p: John points ahead to 12:3. Western tradition later merged this Mary with two other women.
b: The narrator mentions an anointing that he has not yet told (12:1–8), as if the readers already know it, perhaps from the story in Mark 14:3–9. Later readers joined three different women into one. In a sermon of AD 591, Pope Gregory the Great identified Mary of Bethany with the sinful woman who anointed Jesus' feet in Luke 7:36–50 and with Mary Magdalene. That merged figure shaped Western art and preaching for a thousand years. The Eastern churches always kept the three apart, with separate feast days. Most modern scholars, Catholic and Protestant, also keep them apart, and the Catholic calendar has separated them since 1969. The Gospels themselves never call Mary of Bethany a sinner.

a: The man you love is sick.
t: "The one you love": was Lazarus the Beloved Disciple?
p: Lazarus is the only man in John who is said by name to be loved by Jesus. A few scholars think he wrote the Gospel.
b: The sisters do not name their brother. They say only "the man you love" (hon phileis), and 11:5 and 11:36 say the same with both Greek verbs for love, agapaō and phileō. Here the two verbs mean the same thing, and the Plain English Translation renders both as "love" (see 21:15–17, where the difference is debated). From 13:23 on, John speaks of "the disciple whom Jesus loved." Because Lazarus is the only man named as loved by Jesus, some scholars, among them Floyd Filson (1949) and Ben Witherington, have argued that he is that disciple and the source of the Gospel. Most scholars find this unlikely: the Beloved Disciple appears at the Last Supper, where the other Gospels place only the Twelve, and Lazarus is never called a disciple. See the book's introduction for the views on authorship.

a: This sickness is not headed for death.
p: The sickness will kill Lazarus, but death will not be where it ends. Its end is God's glory.
b: Pros thanaton means "toward death," with death as the goal or final outcome (compare "sin that leads to death," 1 John 5:16). Jesus does not say Lazarus will not die; he will. The second half is a purpose clause (hina): the sickness exists so that the Son of God may be glorified. He says death will not have the last word. The real outcome is glory: the sign will show who Jesus is, as his first sign did (2:11). There is a darker irony too. This sign leads straight to the council's decision to kill Jesus (11:53), and in John, Jesus' death is the moment he "will be glorified" (12:23; 13:31). So the sickness of Lazarus is the first step toward the hour of Jesus' glory.
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν πρὸς θάνατον (ouk estin pros thanaton)

a: he stayed on two more days right where he was
p: The delay is deliberate, and it follows a pattern in John: Jesus acts on his Father's timing, not on request.
b: "So" ties the delay to Jesus' love in 11:5, which is startling. Readers have explained it in several ways. Timing: the journey from beyond the Jordan took about a day, and Lazarus has been dead four days when Jesus comes (11:17), so he was probably dead before the messengers arrived. The wait did not cause his death. Pattern: in John, Jesus answers requests on his own terms: his mother at Cana (2:3–7), his brothers at the festival (7:3–10). He acts when the Father's hour comes, not when he is pressed. Purpose: the delay makes the sign greater. A man four days dead is beyond all doubt dead (11:39), and so the sign is "for God's glory" (11:4) and "now you can come to believe" (11:15).

a: the Jews were out to stone you only recently
p: The same Greek word means the authorities who tried to stone Jesus and the friends who mourn with Martha and Mary.
b: Here "the Jews" (hoi Ioudaioi) are the people in Jerusalem who picked up stones against Jesus at the Feast of Dedication (10:31–39). The disciples speaking are Jews themselves, so the word cannot mean the whole Jewish people. It means the Judeans, the people of Jerusalem and Judea, and especially those with power there. In the rest of this chapter the same word names the friends who come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters (11:19, 31), who weep with Mary (11:33), who see Jesus' love (11:36), and many of whom believe in him (11:45). The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek word, as this site does throughout John, and the notes say who is meant. See the topic page on "the Jews" in John.

a: Doesn't the day have twelve hours?
p: Jews and Romans divided daylight into twelve hours, long in summer and short in winter. Jesus has time yet.
b: In the ancient world the time from sunrise to sunset was divided into twelve "hours," whatever the season, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter (compare the parable of the workers, Matthew 20:1–12). Jesus answers the disciples' fear with a proverb: a man walking in daylight does not trip, because he can see. The point is that Jesus' day, the time the Father has given him, is not over yet, so his enemies cannot cut it short (compare 9:4–5, and 7:30; 8:20, "his hour had still not come"). The saying also carries John's larger picture: Jesus is the world's light (8:12), and those without him walk in the dark (11:10; 12:35).

a: has gone to sleep
p: The Bible often calls death "sleep." The disciples miss the meaning, as people often do in John.
b: Kekoimētai, "he has fallen asleep," is a gentle and very old way to speak of death. It is used of the kings of Israel who "slept with their fathers" in the Greek of Kings, of those who "sleep in the dust" in Daniel 12:2, of Stephen (Acts 7:60), and of believers who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–15). Jesus says the same of Jairus' daughter (Mark 5:39). The disciples take him literally, one of the many misunderstandings in John that lead to a clearer word (11:14). Christians have debated what the word implies about the dead before the resurrection; see the card "Where Christians differ" on this chapter.
orig: κεκοίμηται (kekoimētai)

a: he will pull through
p: The Greek says "he will be saved," which in John carries far more than the disciples mean.
b: Sōthēsetai is the ordinary verb for getting well, "he will recover." It is also the verb "be saved." The disciples mean only that sleep is a good sign for a sick man. John's readers hear more: Lazarus will indeed be "saved," but through death and the voice of Jesus, not through rest. The same verb returns in 12:27, where the Plain English Translation renders it "rescue," and in 12:47, "to save the world." The Plain English Translation uses three English words for one Greek verb, so the link is easy to miss.
orig: σωθήσεται (sōthēsetai)

a: Thomas, known as the Twin
p: Thomas is Aramaic for "twin," and Didymus is the Greek word for the same. His words are brave and grim.
b: The Greek says Thomas "who is called Didymus." Te'oma is the Aramaic word for "twin," and didymos is the Greek word for it, so the name is explained for Greek readers. Whose twin he was the Gospels never say. Syriac Christians later called him "Judas Thomas." His first words in John show loyal courage with little hope: if Jesus is going to his death in Judea, they will die with him. John's readers know that when the arrest comes, the disciples scatter (16:32), and that this same Thomas will later doubt, and then make the Gospel's greatest confession (20:24–29).
orig: Θωμᾶς ὁ λεγόμενος Δίδυμος (Thōmas ho legomenos Didymos)

a: already four days in the tomb
p: Jews buried the dead on the day they died. By the fourth day, everyone knew death was final.
b: In the land of Israel's heat, the dead were buried the same day, as Lazarus surely was. Later Jewish writings record a belief that the soul stays near the body for three days, hoping to return, and leaves when the face begins to change (Genesis Rabbah 100:7; Leviticus Rabbah 18:1). These collections are later than John, so the belief cannot be dated with certainty, but it fits the stress on "four days" here and in 11:39. Whatever the belief, the point is plain: there could be no doubt that Lazarus was dead and decaying. Jairus' daughter and the widow's son at Nain were raised the same day they died (Mark 5:35–43; Luke 7:11–17).

a: Bethany was close to Jerusalem
p: Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives' eastern slope. Its Arabic name today, al-Eizariya, comes from Lazarus.
b: Bethany sat on the far side of the Mount of Olives, on the road down to Jericho, about fifteen stadia (under two miles) from the city. Pilgrims coming up from Jericho passed through it on the last stretch to Jerusalem (Mark 11:1). By the 300s Christians showed a tomb of Lazarus there: Eusebius mentions it, and the pilgrim Egeria describes a service at the "Lazarium" on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, a day still kept as Lazarus Saturday in the Eastern churches. The modern Arabic name of the town, al-Eizariya, comes from the Greek Lazarion, "place of Lazarus."

a: comfort the sisters about their brother
p: Visiting and comforting mourners was a duty of love. Mourning lasted seven days, with loud wailing.
b: Jewish mourning lasted seven days after burial (Sirach 22:12), a custom still kept as shiva, "seven." The family stayed at home, sitting on the ground, while friends and neighbors came to comfort them. The rabbis counted comforting mourners among the deeds of loving-kindness. Mourning was loud: the Mishnah says even the poorest man must hire at least two flute players and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral (Mishnah Ketubot 4:4). So the scene is crowded. Many people from Jerusalem, which suggests a family of some standing, sit in the house and go out wailing to the tomb (11:31). That crowd becomes the witness of the sign (11:42, 45).

a: Mary, though, stayed sitting in the house
p: The sisters act here just as they do in Luke's story: Martha active, Mary still.
b: In Luke 10:38–42, Martha is busy serving while Mary sits at Jesus' feet and listens. Here Martha hurries out to meet Jesus and talks with him, while Mary sits in the house (as mourners did) until she is called. At the supper in 12:2–3, Martha serves and Mary is again at Jesus' feet. John and Luke tell different stories, but they paint the same two women. Many see this as a sign that both drew on real memories of the family.

a: at the resurrection on the last day
p: Martha states the hope of most Jews of her day, held especially by the Pharisees: God will raise the dead.
b: Belief in a resurrection at the end of the age had grown from Daniel 12:2 and books like 2 Maccabees 7:9–14. In Jesus' day the Pharisees and most ordinary Jews held it, and the Sadducees denied it (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8). The Mishnah later says that "all Israel has a share in the world to come," except, first of all, "one who says there is no resurrection of the dead" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). The daily prayer of Judaism praises God "who gives life to the dead." So Martha's answer is sound Jewish faith, the faith Jesus himself taught (5:28–29; 6:39–40). What Jesus adds is not a different hope but a person at its center (11:25).

a: I am the resurrection and the life.
p: The end-time hope becomes a person, present now. Scholars differ on how much is now and how much is still future.
b: This is the fifth of John's seven "I am" sayings with a picture (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection and life, way, vine). Martha has placed the resurrection on "the last day" (11:24). Jesus places it in himself, standing in front of her. Two promises follow. Believers who die "will live": they will rise. Believers who are living "will never die": the life he gives does not end at death (11:26). Some (Rudolf Bultmann) read John as moving the hope wholly into the present: eternal life now is the resurrection. Most (Brown, Carson, Keener) note that John keeps both: life now (5:24) and a bodily rising on the last day (5:28–29; 6:40). The raising of Lazarus, a real body leaving a real tomb, is a sign of both.

a: will never die, not ever
t: "Never die": what it does and does not mean
p: The Greek is the strongest denial possible. Yet Lazarus will die again. What is promised is life death cannot end.
b: Ou mē apothanē eis ton aiōna stacks a double negative with "to the age," the strongest way Greek can say "never." It cannot mean that believers will not die physically: Lazarus himself will die again, and the priests will soon plan to kill him (12:10). It means that physical death will not cut them off from the life Jesus gives, which is "eternal life," the life of the age to come (3:16; 5:24; 8:51). Jesus then asks Martha the question the Gospel asks every reader: "Do you believe that?"
orig: οὐ μὴ ἀποθάνῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (ou mē apothanē eis ton aiōna)

a: I have come to believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God
p: Martha says exactly what the Gospel was written to bring readers to believe (20:31).
b: Pepisteuka is a perfect tense: "I have believed and still do." Martha's three titles gather up the Gospel's hopes. "The Messiah" is the anointed king. "The Son of God" is the title the book exists to prove: "so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God" (20:31). "The one coming into the world" echoes "the one who comes" of Psalm 118:26, which the crowd will shout in 12:13 (compare 1:9; 6:14). In the other Gospels, the great confession belongs to Peter (Matthew 16:16). In John it is spoken by a grieving woman before the sign, not after it.
orig: πεπίστευκα (pepisteuka)

a: to wail there
p: The mourners "wail" (klaiō), the loud grief of a funeral. Jesus' tears in 11:35 use a different word.
b: Klaiō is loud weeping, the public lament expected at a death, often with professional mourners (Mark 5:38–39). Mary and the Jews with her are doing this (11:31, 33). In 11:35 John chooses a different verb for Jesus: dakryō, "to shed tears," found only there in the New Testament. The Plain English Translation uses "wail" and "wept" so the reader can see the difference.
orig: κλαύσῃ (klausē), from κλαίω

a: Anger stirred deep in his spirit, and he let himself be shaken
p: The Greek verb means to snort with anger. Most English Bibles soften it to "deeply moved." Why the anger is debated.
b: Embrimaomai was used of a horse snorting, and of people who scold or are indignant (Mark 1:43; 14:5; Matthew 9:30). The KJV has "he groaned in the spirit." Most modern versions say "deeply moved," but the word's normal sense is anger, and the Plain English Translation follows that (again at 11:38). At what? Death and the power behind it, the enemy that has hurt people he loves (B. B. Warfield; many others). Unbelief: the wailing shows no hope in him (some ancient and modern readers). Both: anger at death's grip on the human race, seen in the wailing. The case for "deeply moved": with "in the spirit" the verb may describe a strong inner surge of feeling rather than a scolding, and Jesus has just seen grief, not wrongdoing. "He let himself be shaken" is literally "he troubled himself," the verb of 12:27, 13:21 and 14:1. Augustine made much of the reflexive: we are troubled against our will, but Christ "troubled himself" because he chose to (Tractates on John 49.18).
orig: ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι καὶ ἐτάραξεν ἑαυτόν (enebrimēsato tō pneumati kai etaraxen heauton)

a: Jesus wept.
p: The shortest verse in English Bibles. Jesus sheds quiet tears just before he raises Lazarus.
b: Edakrysen, "he shed tears," is a different word from the wailing of 11:31 and 11:33 (see the note on 11:31). Jesus knows he is about to raise Lazarus, yet he weeps. Readers have taken this in several ways: as grief with his friends (Romans 12:15), as sorrow over death itself, or as the observers take it, love for Lazarus (11:36). Early Christians pointed to this verse against teachers who said Jesus only seemed to be human (Hebrews 4:15; 5:7). It is the shortest verse in most English Bibles, because of where verse numbers were placed in 1551. In Greek, 1 Thessalonians 5:16 is shorter.
orig: ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (edakrysen ho Iēsous)

a: He opened the blind man's eyes.
p: The doubters point back to the sign of chapter 9, a few months earlier in Jerusalem.
b: These Judeans know the healing of the man born blind (9:1–7), which caused a great stir in Jerusalem at the Feast of Booths (9:8–34; 10:21). Their question can be heard as honest puzzlement or as a sneer. John has already given the answer: the sickness is for God's glory (11:4), as the blindness was (9:3).

a: The tomb was a cave. A stone lay on it.
p: Families of some means buried their dead in caves cut into the rock, closed with a heavy stone.
b: Around Jerusalem, families with some means cut burial caves into the soft limestone, with niches or shelves for the bodies. The entrance was closed with a large stone, usually a square plug and sometimes a rolling disk, to keep out animals and robbers. After a year, when the flesh had decayed, the bones were often gathered into a stone box (ossuary). The Greek "lay on it" may mean the stone lay against the opening, or on top of a shaft. The same kind of tomb, with a stone that must be moved, awaits Jesus (20:1; Mark 15:46).

a: he already stinks
p: Martha's words are plain and earthy: the body is decaying. Faith in 11:27 does not mean she expects a miracle now.
b: Literally "he already smells, for he is a fourth-day one." Jewish burial did not embalm the body. Spices and perfumes were placed with it (19:39–40), but they could not stop decay. Martha has confessed Jesus as the Messiah (11:27), yet she cannot imagine what he means to do. Jesus' reply (11:40) ties the moment back to his words in 11:4 and 11:25–26.
orig: ἤδη ὄζει (ēdē ozei)

a: Father, I give you thanks because you heard me.
t: A prayer said aloud for the crowd
p: Jesus thanks God before the sign, then explains that he prays aloud so that the crowd may believe.
b: Jesus gives thanks for an answer already given. Some readers find 11:42 strange, as if the prayer were for show. But Jewish prayer was normally said aloud, and praying so that onlookers may know who has acted is a biblical pattern: Elijah on Mount Carmel prays, "Answer me, LORD! Answer me! Then this people will know that you, LORD, are the God" (1 Kings 18:37). Jesus wants the crowd to see the sign as the Father's work, done through the one he sent, and not as magic. His whole life in John is one of dependence on the Father (5:19, 30). "Raised his eyes upward" is the posture of prayer again in 17:1.

a: Lazarus, come out here!
t: The voice that calls the dead
p: Jesus does here what he promised in 5:25–28: the dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live.
b: Jesus had said that "an hour is coming, and it has arrived now, when the dead will hear the Son of God's voice" (5:25), and that one day "everyone lying in the tombs will hear his voice" (5:28). Here one man in one tomb hears it. The good shepherd also "calls out to his own sheep, each by name" (10:3). The Old Testament prophets Elijah and Elisha raised the dead by long prayer and by stretching themselves on the body (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:32–37); Jesus raises by a word, as in the other Gospels (Mark 5:41; Luke 7:14).

a: His feet and hands were bound with strips of cloth, and a cloth was tied around his face.
t: Grave clothes on and grave clothes off
p: Lazarus comes out bound in his burial wrappings. Jesus will leave his own wrappings behind in the tomb.
b: The body was wrapped in strips of cloth (keiriai), and a separate cloth (soudarion, from Latin sudarium, a sweat cloth) covered the face. Lazarus comes out still bound, and others must untie him. He has been brought back to ordinary life, and he will die again. At Jesus' tomb, the disciples find the linen wrappings lying there and the cloth from his head rolled up separately (20:5–7). Many readers see the contrast as deliberate: Lazarus returns to this life, while Jesus rises to a life death cannot touch.

a: called the council together
p: The Greek word is synedrion, Jerusalem's ruling council under the high priest. How it worked is debated.
b: Synedrion ("sitting together") gives the Hebrew loanword Sanhedrin. In Jesus' day it was the high priest's council in Jerusalem, with chief priests, elders and scribes, and it handled Jewish affairs under Roman oversight. The Mishnah describes a Great Sanhedrin of 71 members with fixed rules of procedure (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6; 4:1), but that picture comes from after AD 70 and is partly ideal. Josephus suggests that the high priest called advisers together as needed. Here the word has no article, "a council," and may mean a meeting rather than a formal court. Many historians, such as E. P. Sanders, think this flexible picture fits the Gospels best.

a: the chief priests and the Pharisees
p: The chief priests were mostly Sadducees, rivals of the Pharisees. John names both as the authorities.
b: In Jesus' time the chief priests, the leading priestly families, held power in Jerusalem and were mostly Sadducees. The Pharisees were a popular lay movement with some members on the council (Acts 5:34; 23:6). John often joins the two (7:32, 45; 11:57; 18:3). Many critical scholars think this reflects John's own day, after AD 70, when the Temple and its priests were gone and Pharisaic teachers led the Jewish communities that John's churches knew. Others point out that leading Pharisees did sit with the priests on councils before 70, as Josephus shows, so the pairing is historically possible. In this scene the chief priests clearly lead (11:49; 12:10).

a: our place and our nation
p: "The place" is the temple. The Romans did destroy it in AD 70, as John's first readers knew.
b: In Jewish speech "the place" often means the temple (Acts 6:13–14; compare "But the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation" (2 Maccabees 5:19)). The leaders fear that a messianic movement will give Rome a reason to crush the temple and the nation's limited self-rule. Their fear was realistic: Rome put down such movements with force, and Josephus tells of several. John's first readers knew the irony. The leaders moved against Jesus to save the place, and in AD 70 the Romans destroyed it anyway.

a: Caiaphas, the high priest in that year
p: Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36. A family tomb with his name may have been found in 1990.
b: Josephus says Joseph "who was called Caiaphas" was made high priest by the Roman governor Valerius Gratus (about AD 18) and removed by the Syrian legate Vitellius (about AD 36 or 37), after Pilate left office (Jewish Antiquities 18.35, 95). His long term suggests he worked well with Pilate. He was the son-in-law of Annas, an earlier high priest (18:13). In 1990 a burial cave in Jerusalem yielded an ornate ossuary inscribed "Yehosef bar Qayafa," Joseph son of Caiaphas. Many think it held the high priest's bones; some doubt the link. "In that year" does not mean the office changed yearly; it means in that fateful year.

a: one man should die on behalf of the people
p: Caiaphas speaks political sense. John hears in his words the meaning of the cross.
b: Caiaphas' logic is the hard logic of power: better one man dead than the nation lost. Jewish law later debated just this question. If enemies demand one person from a town to kill, the town must not hand over any innocent life, but if they name a man already guilty, like Sheba son of Bichri, he may be handed over (Tosefta Terumot 7:20; compare 2 Samuel 20:21–22). Caiaphas does not ask whether Jesus is guilty. John's readers hear his words a second way. "On behalf of" (hyper) is the word of the good shepherd who lays down his life "for the sheep" (10:11, 15) and of the friend who dies for his friends (15:13). John recalls the saying at the trial (18:14).
orig: ἵνα εἷς ἄνθρωπος ἀποθάνῃ ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ (hina heis anthrōpos apothanē hyper tou laou)

a: he spoke a prophecy
t: The high priest who prophesied without knowing it
p: Jews linked prophecy with the high priest's office. Caiaphas speaks truer than he knows, like Balaam.
b: In Israel the high priest once gave God's answers through the Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21). Josephus says the Hasmonean high priest John Hyrcanus had the gift of prophecy (Jewish War 1.68–69), and Philo wrote that the true priest is a prophet (Special Laws 4.192). John does not praise Caiaphas. He says the office, not the man, spoke: God used Caiaphas' scheming words to say what God was doing, as he once used Balaam, who was hired to curse Israel and blessed it instead (Numbers 23–24).

a: to bring God's scattered children together into one
p: The prophets promised that God would gather Israel's scattered people. John widens the promise to all God's children.
b: The hope of a regathering runs through the prophets: God will bring his scattered people home from every land and make them one (Isaiah 43:5–7; Jeremiah 23:3; Ezekiel 37:21–24; Micah 2:12). Jewish prayers of the time asked for it (Sirach 33:13; Sirach 36:16; Psalms of Solomon 17:26–28). "The scattered" (the diaspora) were first of all Jews living outside the land. John's phrase "the children of God" points further: those who receive the Word are given the right to become God's children, "born of God" (1:12–13), and Jesus has "other sheep" to bring into one flock (10:16). The Greeks of 12:20 are the first sign of it. Most interpreters see both groups here, scattered Jews and believing Gentiles.

a: So from that day on they were set on killing him.
t: What set the plot in motion?
p: In John the raising of Lazarus triggers the final plot. In Mark it is the scene in the temple.
b: John has the authorities seeking Jesus' death long before (5:18; 7:1; 8:59), but here the council makes it a formal decision, and the reason is the Lazarus sign. In Matthew, Mark and Luke, the decisive act is Jesus' disruption in the temple courts in his last week (Mark 11:15–18), which John places at the start of the ministry (2:13–22). Some historians find John's account plausible: a sign done two miles from Jerusalem at Passover time, drawing crowds, would alarm the authorities. Others think John has moved the turning point to make the gift of life the cause of Jesus' death, a theme of the whole Gospel.

a: a town named Ephraim
p: Ephraim was probably the village now called Taybeh, on the edge of the desert north of Jerusalem.
b: Most scholars place this Ephraim at et-Taiyibeh (Taybeh), about 12 miles (20 km) north and east of Jerusalem, on high ground above the wilderness that falls toward the Jordan valley. It is probably the Ophrah of Joshua 18:23 and the Ephron of 2 Chronicles 13:19. It was close enough to reach Jerusalem for Passover and remote enough to stay out of reach of the council.

a: among the Jews
p: Here "the Jews" means the people of Judea and their leaders, from whom Jesus withdraws.
b: Jesus himself and his disciples are Jews, so "among the Jews" cannot mean the Jewish people as such. It means Judea and Jerusalem, where the authorities have just resolved to kill him (11:53), as in 7:1, where he stays in Galilee because "the Jews" in Judea seek his life. He withdraws to Ephraim, on the edge of the wilderness, until the Passover. See the note on 11:8.

a: The Passover of the Jews was coming soon.
t: The third Passover, and purifying for it
p: John names three Passovers, which is where the idea of a three-year ministry comes from.
b: John mentions a Passover in 2:13, another in 6:4, and this one, the Passover at which Jesus dies. That is why Christians often speak of a ministry of about three years; the other Gospels mention only one Passover during the ministry. Pilgrims came up early because anyone who had touched a dead body, been in a house with one, or walked over a grave was impure for seven days and had to be sprinkled on the third and seventh days before eating the Passover (Numbers 9:6–12; Numbers 19:11–19; 2 Chronicles 30:17–18). Many ritual baths found around the Temple Mount served the crowds. Irony again: the pilgrims purify themselves while the authorities plot an innocent death (compare 18:28).

a: so they could seize him
p: The authorities issue orders for anyone who knows where Jesus is to report it.
b: The "commands" make Jesus a wanted man. That explains the crowd's question in 11:56 and why Jesus' public arrival in 12:12–19 is so bold. It also prepares for Judas, who will give the authorities what they want: a way to arrest him away from the festival crowds (18:2–3; Mark 14:10–11).

a: six days ahead of the Passover
p: John's dating puts the supper on Saturday evening and the entry on Sunday, the day Christians call Palm Sunday.
b: In John, Jesus dies on the day of preparation, when the Passover lambs were slaughtered, and Passover begins that evening, which was a Sabbath (19:14, 31). Counting back six days puts Jesus' arrival in Bethany around the Sabbath before, the supper perhaps on Saturday evening after the Sabbath ended, and the entry into Jerusalem "on the following day" (12:12), a Sunday. That is the source of Palm Sunday. Mark places the anointing later, "two days" before Passover and after the entry (Mark 14:1–3). Some think John has the true order; others think Mark placed the story beside the plot and Judas' betrayal for its meaning, and that neither Gospel meant to give an exact date.

a: lying at the table
p: At a formal meal guests lay on couches, leaning on the left elbow, with their feet stretched out behind.
b: At festive meals in the Greek and Roman world, which Jews had adopted, guests did not sit on chairs. They reclined on couches or cushions around a low table, leaning on the left elbow and eating with the right hand, their feet stretched out away from the table. The Passover meal was eaten this way as a sign of freedom (compare 13:23–25). That is why Mary could reach Jesus' feet without disturbing the meal. Martha "waited on them" (diēkonei), the same work she does in Luke 10:40.

a: a litra of perfumed oil, real nard and worth a great deal
p: A litra was a Roman pound, about 11.5 ounces. Nard came from a Himalayan plant. The word for "real" is a puzzle.
b: The litra (Latin libra) was the Roman pound, about 327 grams or 11.5 ounces, a very large amount of perfume. Nard (spikenard) is an oil from the root of a plant of the Himalayas, carried to the Mediterranean over long trade routes and very costly (Song of Songs 1:12; 4:13–14). The rare word pistikēs, found only here and in Mark 14:3, is unclear. It may mean "genuine" (from pistis, "trust"), "liquid" (from a verb "to drink"), or a product name, perhaps from the pistachio. Most English Bibles say "pure." That John and Mark share such a rare word suggests that John knew Mark or a tradition close to it.
orig: λίτραν μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτίμου (litran myrou nardou pistikēs polytimou)
r: Mark 14:3; Song of Songs 1:12; Song of Songs 4:13–14

a: She anointed Jesus' feet and dried his feet with her hair
t: One anointing, or two, or three?
p: Mark and Matthew tell of a woman anointing Jesus' head in Bethany; Luke, of a sinful woman in Galilee.
b: Mark 14:3–9 and Matthew 26:6–13: in Bethany, at the house of Simon the leper, two days before Passover, an unnamed woman pours nard on Jesus' head; others object; Jesus speaks of his burial. Luke 7:36–50: in Galilee, early in the ministry, at the house of Simon a Pharisee, a sinful woman wets Jesus' feet with tears, wipes them with her hair, and anoints them. John: in Bethany, six days before Passover, Mary anoints the feet and wipes them with her hair; Judas objects; burial is mentioned. Most scholars think Mark and John tell the same event, and that John's story shares details (feet, hair) with Luke's, either because the stories mixed as they were retold or because John knew both. Others hold there were two anointings. Feet, not head: kings were anointed on the head, but here Mary takes the place of a servant at his feet, as Jesus will at the disciples' feet (13:5).

a: the smell of the oil filled the house
t: A fragrance that fills the house
p: In Mark the woman's deed will be told in all the world. In John its scent fills the whole house.
b: Mark ends the story with Jesus' promise that what the woman did will be told in her memory wherever the good news is preached in the whole world (Mark 14:9). John gives no such saying but an image that does the same work: the scent spreads through the house. Many readers since the church fathers have heard Song of Songs 1:12, where the bride's nard gives off its fragrance while the king is at his table. Paul uses the same picture of the knowledge of Christ spreading like a fragrance (2 Corinthians 2:14–16).
r: Mark 14:9; Song of Songs 1:12; 2 Corinthians 2:14–16; Ephesians 5:2

a: Judas Iscariot
p: "Iscariot" probably means "man of Kerioth." The verb usually rendered "betray" means "hand over."
b: John alone tells us that Judas' father was Simon, also called Iscariot (6:71; 13:26). The most likely meaning of the name is Hebrew ish Qeriyyot, "man of Kerioth," a town in Judah (Joshua 15:25); if so, Judas may have been the only Judean among the Twelve. Other proposals, such as a link with the sicarii ("dagger men") or an Aramaic word for "liar," have fewer supporters. The verb paradidōmi means "hand over" (a prisoner to the authorities, 18:30, 35). English Bibles usually say "betray," which is its sense here. The Plain English Translation keeps "hand over," as at 6:71, because the same verb is used when Pilate hands Jesus over (19:16) and when God gives up his Son (Romans 8:32).
orig: Ἰούδας ὁ Ἰσκαριώτης ... ὁ μέλλων αὐτὸν παραδιδόναι (Ioudas ho Iskariōtēs ... ho mellōn auton paradidonai)

a: three hundred denarii
p: A denarius was a day's pay for a laborer, so the oil was worth about a year's work.
b: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, the normal day's wage for a farm worker (Matthew 20:2). Three hundred denarii, with Sabbaths and festivals off, is about a year's earnings, enough to feed a poor family for a year. Mark says "over three hundred denarii" (Mark 14:5). Giving to the poor was expected at Passover, which is why, at the last supper, some disciples think Judas has gone out to give something to them (13:29).

a: He held the common purse and would take for himself what people put in it
p: Only John says Judas stole from the group's money. The verb for "take" also means "carry," a wordplay.
b: The glōssokomon was a box or bag for keeping money (also 13:29). Jesus and his disciples lived partly on gifts (Luke 8:1–3) and gave to the poor from the shared purse. The verb ebastazen normally means "he carried," but in Greek papyri it can also mean "he carried off," that is, stole. John seems to use both senses: he carried the purse, and he helped himself from it. The other Gospels say Judas was paid to hand Jesus over (Mark 14:10–11; Matthew 26:14–16), but only John calls him a thief.
orig: τὰ βαλλόμενα ἐβάσταζεν (ta ballomena ebastazen)

a: for the day of my burial
p: The Greek ties "Let her be" to a puzzling "so that she may keep it." The KJV reads a different text.
b: The oldest text reads aphes autēn, hina eis tēn hēmeran tou entaphiasmou mou tērēsē auto, word for word "let her alone, so that for the day of my burial she may keep it." The Plain English Translation keeps that link. If Mary has just poured out the whole pound, what is left to keep? Interpreters take it in three main ways. (1) She may keep what is left for the burial itself (on this view she used only part). (2) She was meant to keep it for the day of his burial, and today counts as that day: she has anointed his body ahead of time, as Mark 14:8 says. Many English versions paraphrase this way. (3) A few interpreters read "keep" as "observe": let her keep this act in view of his burial. Later manuscripts smooth the line to "she has kept this," which the KJV follows (see the variant). The anointing becomes the first act of Jesus' burial, completed by Nicodemus with a hundred pounds of spices (19:39–40).
orig: ἵνα εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ ἐνταφιασμοῦ μου τηρήσῃ αὐτό

a: you always have poor people among you
p: Jesus echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, a law that commands generosity. It is not a shrug at poverty.
b: The saying recalls Deuteronomy 15:11: "For there will never stop being people in need in the land. That is why I am commanding you: Open your hand wide to your brother, to the poor and the needy among you in your land" (Deuteronomy 15:11). The law's point is that poverty will last, so generosity must last too. Jesus does not set the poor against himself. Mark's form adds, "you are able to help them whenever you wish" (Mark 14:7). His point is the moment: he will soon be gone, and Mary has seen it. The wording here matches Matthew 26:11, whose Greek is nearly the same. The verse has often been misused to argue that nothing can be done about poverty. In its source, it is the reason to give.

a: So the chief priests decided to kill Lazarus too
t: Why do the other Gospels not tell of Lazarus?
p: The greatest sign in John is missing from Matthew, Mark and Luke. Scholars explain the silence in several ways.
b: If the raising of Lazarus led to the plot against Jesus (11:53), why do the other Gospels not mention it? Protective silence: Richard Bauckham argues that Mark's tradition left Lazarus, and the woman who anointed Jesus, unnamed or untold because they were still in danger in Jerusalem, as this verse shows. Once they had died, John could name them. Different scope: the other Gospels focus on Galilee and tell almost nothing of Jesus' visits to Judea before his last week; they report raisings of the dead too (Mark 5:35–43; Luke 7:11–17). A Johannine story: many critical scholars think John built the account from older material, perhaps influenced by Luke's sisters (Luke 10:38–42) and the parable of Lazarus, whose last line is that some will not believe "even if someone rises from the dead" (Luke 16:31). See the chapter page on chapter 11.

a: many Jews were drifting away
p: Many Judeans were leaving the leaders' side and going over to Jesus, a sign the movement was growing near Jerusalem.
b: Hypēgon means "they were going away": leaving their homes for Bethany, or, as most read it, leaving the authorities' camp. Again "the Jews" here, as in "a great crowd of the Jews" in 12:9, are Judeans, many of whom believe in Jesus (compare 11:45; 12:42). The plot against Lazarus shows how John sees the authorities: willing to kill a man whose only offense is to be alive.
orig: ὑπῆγον (hypēgon)

a: They took fronds from the palm trees
t: Palm branches: a sign of victory
p: Only John mentions palms. In Jewish memory they marked national victory, as when the Maccabees retook Jerusalem.
b: Palm branches were carried at the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:40; Nehemiah 8:15). They also stood for victory and national hope. When Simon the Maccabee took the Citadel of Jerusalem in 141 BC, "he entered it with praise and palm branches" (1 Maccabees 13:51), and the temple was rededicated with palm branches and hymns (2 Maccabees 10:7). Palm trees later appeared on Jewish coins of the revolts against Rome. So the crowd greets Jesus as a liberator king. Mark mentions leafy branches cut from the fields, Matthew branches from the trees, and Luke only cloaks on the road (Mark 11:8; Matthew 21:8; Luke 19:36). Revelation's great crowd holds palms before the Lamb (Revelation 7:9).
r: Leviticus 23:40; Nehemiah 8:15; 1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7; Revelation 7:9; Mark 11:8; Matthew 21:8; Luke 19:36

a: Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name
p: "Hosanna" is Hebrew for "save, please!" The crowd sings Psalm 118, a Passover psalm, and adds "the King of Israel."
b: Hōsanna represents Hebrew hoshi'a na, "save, please!": "LORD, please, save us now!" (Psalm 118:25). By Jesus' time it had become a shout of praise as well as a plea. The next line is Psalm 118:26: "Blessed is the one who comes in the LORD's name!" (Psalm 118:26). Psalm 118 closes the Hallel, the psalms sung at Passover and the Feast of Booths, so pilgrims knew it by heart. The Greek has "Lord" (kyrios) where the Hebrew has the divine name. The crowd adds "the King of Israel," Nathanael's title for Jesus (1:49), which turns a pilgrim's blessing into a royal welcome. The same psalm gives the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22; Mark 12:10).

a: Jesus found a little donkey and sat on it
p: In John, Jesus mounts the donkey after the crowd hails him as king, as if to show what kind of king he is.
b: In the other Gospels Jesus sends two disciples ahead to bring the animal, and the crowd's welcome follows (Mark 11:1–10; Matthew 21:1–9; Luke 19:28–38). John gives no such account: the crowd comes out first, hailing a King of Israel with palms of victory, and then Jesus "found" a little donkey. Many interpreters (Brown, Lincoln) read this as Jesus' answer to the crowd: he is a king, but not the warrior they hoped for. Zechariah's king rides a donkey and "will cut off the chariot ... and the war horse" and speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:9–10). Others think the order simply reflects John's shorter telling. Solomon rode David's mule to be anointed king (1 Kings 1:33–38), so a donkey could be a royal mount too.

a: Daughter of Zion, have no fear.
p: John quotes Zechariah 9:9 in brief. "Have no fear" replaces Zechariah's "Rejoice greatly."
b: Zechariah 9:9 begins "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem!" and describes the king as righteous, saving and humble. John's short form begins instead with "have no fear," perhaps from Zephaniah 3:16, where Zion is told not to fear because "The LORD, Israel's King, is in your midst" (Zephaniah 3:15–16), or from Isaiah 40:9. "Daughter of Zion" is a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people. Matthew quotes the verse more fully and has two animals, a donkey and its colt, reading the Hebrew parallel lines literally (Matthew 21:2–7). John, like Mark and Luke, has one. Where the Greek is the same as Matthew's ("Look, your king is coming"), the Plain English Translation uses Matthew's wording.

a: But once Jesus had been glorified, they remembered
p: John says openly that the disciples understood these events only later, after the resurrection.
b: Twice John says the disciples grasped the meaning of an event only after Jesus was raised and glorified (2:22; 12:16), and Jesus promises that the Spirit will remind them of all he said (14:26). Many readers see here the Gospel's honest method: its story is told in the light of Easter, and it says so. Critical scholars stress that this hindsight shaped how the stories were told and which Scriptures were linked to them. Others note that remembering is not inventing: the Gospel claims the events came first and the understanding later (compare 21:24).

a: The world has gone off after him!
p: The Pharisees exaggerate in frustration, and John's next verse proves them right: Greeks come.
b: Ho kosmos, "the world," is a common exaggeration ("everybody"). The Pharisees mean only that the crowds are with Jesus. But in John, the world is what God loved and Jesus came to save (3:16–17; 12:47), and the very next verse brings Greeks, people from the wider world, asking to see him (12:20–21). Like Caiaphas (11:50–52), the opponents say more than they know.
orig: ὁ κόσμος ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ ἀπῆλθεν (ho kosmos opisō autou apēlthen)

a: were Greeks
p: These "Greeks" were Gentiles, probably God-fearers who worshiped Israel's God.
b: Hellēnes in the New Testament means non-Jews, Gentiles of Greek culture (7:35; Acts 14:1; Romans 1:16). Greek-speaking Jews are called Hellēnistai (Acts 6:1). These Greeks have "come up to worship," so they are probably God-fearers, Gentiles drawn to Israel's God who attended synagogue and came to the festivals, like the Ethiopian official or Cornelius (Acts 8:27; 10:2). At the temple they could go only as far as the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, where a stone warning barred them from going further on pain of death. Their arrival is the signal for Jesus' hour (12:23).

a: Philip, from Bethsaida in Galilee
p: Philip and Andrew both have Greek names and came from Bethsaida, a town on the edge of the Greek-speaking world.
b: Philip and Andrew are the only two of the Twelve with purely Greek names, and both came from Bethsaida (1:44), a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. It lay just east of the Jordan in the territory of Herod Philip, among many Greek-speaking Gentiles, though people commonly counted it as part of Galilee. Greek visitors would naturally turn to such men. Their request, "we want to see Jesus," uses John's word for the seeing that leads to faith (1:39, 46; 14:9).

a: The hour is here
p: All through John, Jesus' "hour" has not yet come. Now, at the Greeks' request, it arrives.
b: From Cana on, Jesus says "My hour is not here yet" (2:4), and the narrator explains that no one could arrest him "since his hour had still not come" (7:30; 8:20). Now the clock strikes: "The hour is here" (12:23, 27), and again before the supper (13:1) and in his prayer (17:1). The hour is the whole event of his death, rising and return to the Father, which John calls his being "glorified" or "lifted up." That the Greeks' coming opens the hour fits 12:32: once lifted up, he will draw everyone.
orig: ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα (elēlythen hē hōra)

a: if a grain of wheat does not fall into the earth and die
p: A seed must be buried to bear fruit. Jesus applies the picture to his own death, and Paul to the resurrection.
b: A grain kept in the barn remains a single grain. Buried in the ground, it "dies" and rises as a stalk carrying many grains. Jesus uses the farmer's picture for his death, which will bear "a lot of fruit," the many who come to him, Greeks among them. Paul uses the same picture for the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:36–38). The rabbis used it too: the Talmud has Rabbi Meir argue that if a grain of wheat buried bare comes up clothed, how much more will the righteous rise clothed (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 90b). The saying then widens in 12:25–26 to every follower.

a: hate their life
p: "Love" and "hate" here are Hebrew ways of saying "put first" and "put second," not a call to self-loathing.
b: In Hebrew idiom, to "love" one and "hate" another often means to prefer one to the other (Genesis 29:30–31; Malachi 1:2–3; compare Luke 14:26 with Matthew 10:37). The word for life is psychē, a person's own life or self. Jesus is not telling people to despise themselves but to value his way more than their own survival. The saying appears in every Gospel, in different forms (Mark 8:35; Matthew 10:39; 16:25; Luke 9:24; 17:33). John alone adds "in this world" and "into eternal life," setting this present life against the life of the age to come.
orig: ὁ μισῶν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ (ho misōn tēn psychēn autou)
r: Mark 8:35; Matthew 10:37–39; Matthew 16:25; Luke 9:24; Luke 14:26; Luke 17:33; Genesis 29:30–31

a: My soul is shaken now.
p: John has no prayer in the garden. Instead, Jesus' anguish and his choice come here, before the crowd.
b: In Mark, Jesus says in Gethsemane, "my soul is very sorrowful," and prays that the hour might pass and the cup be taken away (Mark 14:34–36). John gives no such scene, but this verse holds the same struggle. "My soul is shaken" may echo the Greek of the Psalms of lament (Psalm 6:3; Psalm 42:6). Then: is "Father, rescue me from this hour" a prayer Jesus actually prays, or one he considers and rejects? The Greek manuscripts have no punctuation, so editors must decide. The SBLGNT, this site's base text, prints it as a real request ending with a period, and the KJV also prints it as a prayer. Many editions and most modern English versions print it as a question, and commentators divide. The Plain English Translation prints a question because the next words begin with "but" (alla) and answer a proposal just set aside: "But this is exactly why I have come to this hour." Read as a real prayer, the verse shows Jesus asking and then yielding, as in Gethsemane. Either way, the verse shows real fear and a free choice (compare 10:18; 18:11; Hebrews 5:7).

a: Then a voice came out of heaven
p: This is John's only voice from heaven. The other Gospels have one at the baptism and the transfiguration.
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of a voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism and on the mountain of transfiguration (Mark 1:11; 9:7), scenes John does not narrate. John has this one, at the start of the hour. Later rabbis spoke of the bat qol, "daughter of a voice," an echo from heaven by which God still spoke after the prophets had ceased. "I have glorified it" looks back to the signs and the whole ministry (2:11; 11:4, 40; 17:4); "I will glorify it again" looks to the cross and resurrection.

a: Some said there had been thunder.
p: In the Bible God's voice is often heard as thunder. The crowd hears the sound but not the meaning.
b: At Sinai "God kept answering him with a voice" (Exodus 19:19). The Hebrew word qol means both "voice" and "thunder," and the psalms describe the LORD's voice thundering over the waters (Psalm 29:3; 2 Samuel 22:14; Job 37:4–5). Some in the crowd hear only noise; others think an angel spoke. Similar splits happen in Acts, where Paul's companions hear a sound but do not understand the voice (Acts 9:7; 22:9). Jesus says the voice was for them (12:30), yet most miss it. The scene prepares for 12:37–40.
r: Exodus 19:16–19; 2 Samuel 22:14; Psalm 29:3–9; Job 37:4–5; Acts 9:7; Acts 22:9; Revelation 10:3–4

a: Now this world's ruler will be thrown out.
t: The ruler of this world thrown out
p: "The ruler of this world" is Satan. John sees the cross as his defeat.
b: John uses "the ruler of this world" three times (12:31; 14:30; 16:11). It means the devil, whom Paul calls "the god of this age" (2 Corinthians 4:4) and who in Revelation is "thrown down" from heaven (Revelation 12:9–10). In John, the cross looks like the world's judgment on Jesus but is really the world's judgment and Satan's defeat. This theme, Christ's victory over the powers through his death, was strong in the church fathers and was named "Christus Victor" by the Swedish theologian Gustaf Aulén (1931). Most traditions hold it alongside other ways of explaining the cross, such as sacrifice and substitution.
r: 14:30; 16:11; 16:33; Luke 10:18; 2 Corinthians 4:4; Ephesians 2:2; Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14; Revelation 12:9–10

a: if I am lifted up from the earth
p: The verb means both "raised up" on a cross and "exalted." Isaiah's servant is "lifted up and glorified."
b: Hypsoō means "lift up, raise high," and also "exalt." John uses it three times of Jesus (3:14; 8:28; 12:32), and 12:33 makes clear that it means his death by crucifixion, raised on a cross like the bronze snake on its pole (3:14; Numbers 21:9). It also means his exaltation to glory. The Greek of Isaiah 52:13 has the same pair John uses: God's servant "will be lifted up and glorified" (hypsōthēsetai kai doxasthēsetai), at the head of the song of the suffering servant that John quotes in 12:38. The cross is the place of shame, and in John it is also the throne. "If" (ean) here has the sense "when."
orig: ἐὰν ὑψωθῶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς (ean hypsōthō ek tēs gēs)

a: I will draw everyone to myself
p: Does "everyone" mean all kinds of people, every single person, or all who will finally be saved? Churches differ.
b: "Draw" (helkyō) is the verb of 6:44: "Nobody is able to come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him" (6:44). Here the Son draws "everyone" (pantas). Read in context, the Greeks of 12:20 are the first sign of it: Jews and Gentiles alike will come to the crucified one. Christians disagree about how far "everyone" reaches and whether the drawing can be resisted. Some ancient manuscripts read "all things" (see the variant). For how the traditions answer, see the card "Where Christians differ" on this chapter.
orig: πάντας ἑλκύσω πρὸς ἐμαυτόν (pantas helkysō pros emauton)

a: We have heard the Law say that the Messiah remains forever.
p: No single verse says this, but Psalm 89 promises David's line will last forever. The crowd cannot fit it with a cross.
b: "The Law" here means the Scriptures in general (as in 10:34; 15:25). The likeliest source is Psalm 89, which promises that David's offspring will last forever: "His offspring will go on for all time" (Psalm 89:36), in the Greek "will remain forever" (Psalm 88:37 in the Septuagint), the same verb as here. Other passages spoke of an everlasting reign (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 9:7; Ezekiel 37:25; Daniel 7:14; Psalm 110:4). A Messiah who is "lifted up" and dies did not fit these hopes. Some later Jewish writings did imagine a Messiah who dies (4 Ezra 7:28–29), but after a long reign.
r: Psalm 89:3–4; Psalm 89:36–37; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 9:7; Ezekiel 37:25; Daniel 7:13–14; Psalm 110:4; 4 Ezra 7:28–29

a: Who is this Son of Man?
p: The crowd's question shows that "Son of Man" was not a known title for the Messiah. Jesus does not answer directly.
b: Jesus has just said "the Son of Man will be glorified" (12:23) and "if I am lifted up" (12:32). The crowd puts the two together and is puzzled. Their question suggests that "the Son of Man," Jesus' favorite way of speaking of himself, was not a fixed title that everyone took to mean "the Messiah." It points back to the "one like a son of man" who receives an everlasting kingdom in Daniel 7:13–14. Jesus answers not with a definition but with a call to walk in the light while it lasts (12:35–36).
orig: τίς ἐστιν οὗτος ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου; (tis estin houtos ho huios tou anthrōpou)

a: sons of light
p: A Hebrew idiom for people who belong to the light. The Dead Sea Scrolls used it of their own community.
b: "Sons of" in Hebrew idiom means "people marked by" something. The phrase "sons of light" was used by the community of the Dead Sea Scrolls for its members, set against the "sons of darkness" in the War Scroll and the Community Rule (1QS 1:9–10; 3:13–4:26). The New Testament uses it of believers (Luke 16:8; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). John's light and darkness belong to the same Jewish world of thought, though here a person, not a law or a community, is the light.

a: Jesus went away and was hidden from them
p: The public ministry ends. The light that was "among you" withdraws, as Jesus had warned.
b: Jesus' last public words in the story end with his withdrawal. As at 8:59, he "was hidden," and the warning of 12:35 comes true at once: the light is among them only a short time. From here on John reports no more signs in public and no more teaching to the crowds (12:44–50 is a summary). Chapters 13–17 belong to the disciples alone.

a: Lord, who has believed the report we gave?
p: John quotes the Greek of Isaiah 53:1, the opening of the song of the suffering servant.
b: The quotation matches the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus, word for word, including the address "Lord," which the Hebrew does not have. Isaiah 53 is the song of the servant who is despised and rejected, wounded for others' sins, and "lifted up and glorified" (Isaiah 52:13, Greek). John uses its first line to explain the unbelief of Jesus' hearers: the prophet himself had foreseen that the message about the servant would not be believed. Paul cites the same verse for the same purpose (Romans 10:16). "The Lord's arm" means his power, which Jesus' signs revealed. This site's Isaiah 53:1 reads "Who has believed what we have heard?" (Isaiah 53:1): the Greek akoē, like the Hebrew, can mean either what was heard or the message given. In John the speaker is the messenger whose report was refused, so the Plain English Translation says "the report we gave."

a: He has made their eyes blind and their heart hard
p: John's wording differs from both the Hebrew and the Greek of Isaiah 6:10: here God himself blinds and hardens.
b: In the Hebrew of Isaiah 6:10 God commands the prophet: make the people's heart fat, their ears heavy and their eyes shut. In the Septuagint the people's heart "has grown dull" by itself. John's form has God ("he") blind their eyes and harden their heart, and leaves out the ears. The verse is used across the New Testament to explain why many in Israel did not believe (Mark 4:12; Matthew 13:14–15; Acts 28:26–27; Romans 11:7–10). In each place the hardening is partial and serves a larger purpose (Romans 11:11, 25). The last words are a future in the best Greek texts, kai iasomai, "and I will heal them" (the Byzantine text has a subjunctive). Most take it as still part of the "so that ... not" clause, as the Plain English Translation does; some read it as breaking free of it, a promise: "And I will heal them." The Aramaic Targum of Isaiah softened the verse's end to "and it be forgiven them." On how Christians answer the hard question it raises, see the card on this chapter.
orig: τετύφλωκεν αὐτῶν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ ἐπώρωσεν αὐτῶν τὴν καρδίαν

a: he had seen his glory
p: John says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory. Most take this of Isaiah's temple vision in Isaiah 6.
b: In Isaiah 6 the prophet sees the Lord "sitting on a throne, high and lifted up" (Isaiah 6:1) and cries, "with my own eyes I have seen the King, the LORD of Armies!" (Isaiah 6:5). The Aramaic Targum of Isaiah says he saw "the glory" of the LORD. John says Isaiah saw "his glory," and the context makes "him" Jesus (12:37, 42). Most interpreters conclude that John identifies the glory Isaiah saw on the throne with the pre-existent Son (compare 1:14, 18; 8:56). Richard Bauckham adds a link to Isaiah 52:13, where the servant is "high and lifted up," the words of Isaiah 6:1: Isaiah saw the glory of the one who would be exalted through suffering. Some read "his" as God's glory, seen in its plan for Christ.

a: so they would not be thrown out of the synagogue
p: John three times speaks of believers being put out of the synagogue. When and how this happened is debated.
b: Aposynagōgos, "put out of the synagogue," appears only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). J. Louis Martyn (1968) argued that it reflects John's own day, when a Jewish prayer against heretics, the Birkat ha-Minim, said to have been revised at Yavneh around AD 85, drove Jewish believers in Jesus out of synagogues; the stories, on this view, tell the community's experience. Many scholars now doubt that link: the prayer's early wording and date are uncertain, its target was not mainly Christians, and there was no central authority to enforce it (Reuven Kimelman; Adele Reinhartz; Daniel Boyarin). Local exclusions, of the kind Paul both carried out and suffered, may lie behind the word (2 Corinthians 11:24). John also says that many leaders believed, including Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea (3:1–2; 19:38–39).

a: They loved the glory people give more than the glory God gives.
p: Doxa means both "glory" and "reputation." The rulers chose a good name with people over the glory Isaiah saw.
b: Doxa can mean God's glory, as in 12:41, or human praise and reputation. John plays on both senses: Isaiah saw Christ's glory, but the rulers preferred their standing. Jesus had said the same: "How are you able to believe? You take glory from each other" (5:44). The fear is real: losing one's place in the synagogue meant losing family ties, business and community. John's verdict is still sharp.
orig: τὴν δόξαν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ... τὴν δόξαν τοῦ θεοῦ

a: he is looking at the one who sent me
p: Jewish law said a man's agent is like the man himself. In John the Son is the Father's agent, and more.
b: Jewish law had a principle of agency: "a man's agent is like the man himself" (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5). A messenger (shaliach) acting for someone carried that person's authority. John uses this language often: Jesus is "sent" by the Father, so to receive, honor, believe or see him is to receive, honor, believe or see the Father (5:23; 13:20). John goes further than agency: "The one who has seen me has seen the Father" (14:9), because the Son is one with the Father (10:30) and makes him known (1:18).

a: I came to save the world, not to judge it.
p: Jesus came to save, not to condemn. Yet rejecting him brings judgment. John holds both.
b: This echoes 3:17: God did not send his Son to condemn the world but to save it. Yet Jesus also says the Father has given him all judgment (5:22, 27) and "I came into this world to bring judgment" (9:39). Most readers resolve it as purpose and result: Jesus came to save, but a light that comes into the world shows up the darkness, and those who turn from it judge themselves (3:18–21). 12:48 makes the same point: the word he spoke will be the judge.

a: The word I have spoken is what will judge him on the last day.
p: Jesus' closing words echo God's promise of a prophet like Moses who will speak only God's words.
b: God promised Moses: "I will put my words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him. Anyone who does not listen to my words, which he will speak in my name, I myself will call to account" (Deuteronomy 18:18–19). Jesus' summary follows that pattern closely: he does not speak from himself, the Father commanded him what to say (12:49), and those who refuse his words will answer for it (12:48). Some in the crowds had called him "the Prophet" (6:14; 7:40). In Deuteronomy, too, God's command is life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20; 32:47), as in 12:50.
